div.head: II Atr 7
div.ab: ⁊ gif man secge on landesmann, þæt he orf stæle oððon man sloge, ⁊ hit secge an sceiðman ⁊ an landesman, ðonne ne beo he nane[s] andsæces wyrðe.
Si dicatur in compatriota, quod furtum fecerit uel hominem occiderit, et hoc dicat unus sceidmannus et unus landesmannus, tunc non sit aliqua negatione dignus.
[Be landesmannes tyhte.] ⁊ gif man secge on landesmann þæt he orf stæle oððon man sloge, ⁊ hit secge an sceiðman ⁊ an landesman, ðonne ne beo he nane[s] andsæces wyrðe.

(Von Klage gegen einen [Englischen] Landesunterthan. Ld) Und wenn ein Landesangehöriger angeklagt wird, dass er Vieh gestohlen oder einen Menschen erschlagen habe, und dies sagt [eidlich] aus Ein Schiffsmann [der Nordleute] und Ein Landesangehöriger, dann werde [Verklagt]er zu keinem Reinigungsbeweise zugelassen.

(Of a charge against an [English] native. Ld) And if a native is accused of having stolen cattle or killed a man, and one shipman [of the Northmen] and one native say so [on oath], then let [the accused] not be allowed any denial.

And if a man of our country is charged with having stolen cattle or with having slain anyone, and the charge is brought by one Viking and one man belonging to this country, he shall not be entitled to make any denial.
And if anyone charges a man of our country that he stole cattle or slew a man, and the charge is brought by one viking and one man of this country, he is then to be entitled to no denial.

scegð entlehnt das Agsächsische 10. Jhs. dem Norden, wo es ein langes, schmales, schnelles Schiff besonderer Art bezeichnet; Steenstrup Danelag 155; Stevenson Crawford char. 128; Weinhold Altnord. Leben 137. Über scægðmann (Synonyma s. Gl Dänen 1) vgl. Plummer Saxon chron. II 185.—Die Beweisnähe (s. d. Gl 10b) gehört hier der Klage, die als besonders stark, den Beklagten einem Handhaften (s. d. Gl 6) gleich zu behandeln erlaubt

Anglo-Saxon of the 10th cent. borrows scegð from the North, where it denotes a long, narrow, fast ship of a particular kind; Steenstrup Danelag 155; Stevenson Crawford char. 128; Weinhold Altnord. Leben 137. On scægðmann (for synonyms see Gl Dänen 1) cf. Plummer Saxon chron. II 185. — The right to proof (see that word in Gl 10b) belongs here to the accusation, which, being especially strong, allows the accused to be treated like one taken in the act (see that word in Gl 6)
landesmann, i.e. Englishman as opposed to a member of the invading force, cf. twegen landesmenn and an ælþeodig, Ælfric, Homilies, ed. Thorpe, ii. p. 26, l. 20.

sceiðman is derived from scegð (O. Norse skeið), a light, swift ship of a special kind (see Napier and Stevenson, Crawford Charters, p. 128), probably commonly used by the invaders (see Plummer, Sax. Chr. ii. p. 185), hence the name applied to them, cf. sæmann, flotman, æscmann etc.
